title: What Is Your Fallback Position
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article makes the case that every major decision or negotiation should be entered with a pre-established fallback position — the lowest acceptable outcome a leader is willing to accept if the primary plan collapses. It carefully distinguishes a fallback position from a contingency plan, noting contingencies address foreseeable risk while fallbacks address outright failure or collapse. The piece explains the practical benefits: reduced downtime, less reputational damage, and faster recovery, because the alternative path is decided before the crisis hits rather than improvised during it. It ends by framing the fallback position as a parachute packed in advance, valuable mainly for the confidence it provides even when never used.
points: A fallback position is distinct from a contingency plan: contingencies manage risk before failure, fallbacks define what to do after failure or collapse.
Having a fallback in place before a decision or negotiation minimizes downtime, financial loss, and reputational damage when things go wrong.
In negotiations specifically, a known fallback makes leaders less likely to accept unfavorable terms out of desperation.
The value of a fallback is partly psychological — the confidence of having a plan B, even unused, changes how leaders enter high-stakes decisions.
quotes: Technically speaking, a fallback position is an alternative option or the lowest acceptable outcome the leader is willing to accept if things go terribly wrong.
Don’t confuse a fallback position with a contingency plan. Contingency plans are about risk, not failure.
Fallback plans are about failure, collapse, and defeat. If X is no longer possible or feasible, then the team resorts to fallback position Y.
It is the parachute they pack themselves just in case the plane can’t fly.
For every major decision, what is your fallback position? Sometimes, decisions and strategies blow up. Knowing your fallback position or plan can be a lifesaver.
